title: At least 68 killed in Indonesia quake as aftershocks hamper rescue efforts

Topic:Earthquakes

People are sheltering in makeshift tent amid fears of aftershocks. (AP: Firdia Lisnawati)

At least 68 people have been killed and 200 injured following a magnitude-7.7 earthquake in Indonesia.

Nearly 1,600 aftershocks have been detected in the province since the powerful earthquake struck, with thousands of people sheltering in tents and government buildings afraid to return home.

Displaced people have been awaiting aid for some days but organisations say access to isolated communities is starting to improve.

The number of people killed in a powerful earthquake in eastern Indonesia has risen to 68 as rescue workers continue to search for people trapped under rubble.

Almost 13,000 people have been evacuated following the country's deadliest disaster since 2022, with many sheltering in tents outdoors or at schools and police stations afraid to return to their homes due to fears of aftershocks.

Nearly 1,600 aftershocks have been detected in East Nusa Tenggara province since Saturday, when the magnitude-7.7 quake hit the Indonesian island of Flores.

One of the most prominent, a 5.6 magnitude earthquake, was recorded on Monday morning, local time, according to the country's geophysics agency.

A school has been damaged in Reo, East Nusa Tenggara province. (AP: Firdia Lisnawati)

An official at Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency, Berton SP Panjaitan, confirmed the death toll had risen to 68, up from 54, on Monday night, local time, and that more than 200 people had been injured.

More than 1,300 homes have been damaged, with nearly 250 destroyed on Flores alone, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.

Military and police officers have been deployed across the disaster zone, supported by 10 aircraft to distribute 275 tonnes of aid to the area.

But logistical challenges have slowed deliveries to some hard-hit communities, according to Abdul Muhari, deputy chief of the country's disaster management agency.

A church in Ruteng, Manggarai regency, in the East Nusa Tenggara province, has been damaged in the quake. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

Ridwan Sobri Carman, head of disaster management at Indonesian Red Cross, said access to isolated communities had started to improve which meant they could help with evacuation efforts and providing first aid.

"Our team is also working with the local authorities in seven districts to reach communities affected by landslides," he told the ABC's The World program.

He said while the worst of the damage had occurred in Flores, some islands close by had also been affected.

Patients are treated in a makeshift tent outside a hospital amid fears of aftershocks in Ruteng, East Nusa Tenggara province. (AP: Firdia Lisnawati)

The National Disaster Management Agency was working with federal and international agencies on the disaster response and an emergency fund, according to Ridwan Sobri Carman.

"Our houses are no longer liveable, because many have collapsed and are full of cracks, so we can't go inside anymore," Mbay resident Junaidin told AFP outside a self-made tent that was sleeping about 30 people.

"We only go back home to get water, clothes, pillows, and then we … spend the nights here."

Authorities have also set up two emergency field hospitals in the worst-hit town of Ruteng to treat victims after local hospitals were damaged, with two crisis management teams overseeing a health emergency operation centre, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.

Helmi Yanati is sheltering outside her damaged house following the earthquake, in Poco village, Manggarai regency. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

During Indonesia's Independence Day ceremony in Jakarta, President Prabowo Subianto asked for people to pray for those affected by disasters in East Nusa Tenggara and other parts of the country, while leading a nationwide moment of silence honouring the nation's independence heroes.

But those affected by the disaster have called on the government to do more.

"As for help from the government, there hasn't been any — no tents, no medicine, no food, no drinking water, nothing," said Junaidin, who only has one name.

"Please open your eyes, government. We are your people, we are part of you. So please look after us."
